### Observed differences

- All six qualifying items concern how work on activities was distributed over resources: the resource family produced 6 qualifying items where about 0.003 would be expected if nothing had changed (roughly 2,000 times the chance expectation), while the control-flow family produced 0 of 40 tested units (about 0.2 expected) and the timing family 0 of 34 (about 0.017 expected). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- In the earlier window, work on each of the six activities was spread broadly, with the largest single resources handling about 9–11 assignments in 100 (User_18 was the top or near-top handler of A01, A03 and A22, and one lead resource held about 10–11 in 100 for A13, A14 and A17). In the later window, a largely different set of resources holds the top shares: User_41 leads A01, A03 and A22 with about 9–11 in 100, and the remaining top positions are filled by resources that were previously minor or unlisted (about 4–8 in 100 each). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- For A13, A14 and A17, User_27's share grew roughly fourfold, from about 5 assignments in 100 to about 18–19 in 100, making it the single largest handler; the previous lead resource fell to about 6–7 in 100 and the pooled remainder shrank from about 44–47 in 100 to about 36–38 in 100, so allocation became noticeably more concentrated. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005]
- For A01, A03 and A22, User_18 and a group of roughly eight other previously frequent resources dropped out of the listed contributors (individual shares below about 4 in 100), their place taken by User_41 and several previously minor resources. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN006]
- The profile shifts measure 0.37–0.51 in cosine dissimilarity, and each is larger than about 999.5 of 1,000 random re-splits of the pooled data; the profiles rest on roughly 120–330 assignment observations per window, so they are not based on a handful of cases. ASSIGN003 and ASSIGN004 carry identical profiles for A13 and A14 and therefore reflect one underlying difference rather than two. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that, in the later window, the handling of activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was reallocated from one group of resources to another: resources that previously each carried roughly 5–10 assignments in 100 — including User_18 — withdrew from the top contributors, a new group including User_41 took on comparable shares, and User_27 became the dominant handler of A13, A14 and A17 (about 18–19 in 100, up from about 5 in 100). The support is direct, since the indicator measures exactly these allocation shares, and consistent, since the same resources decline and the same resources rise across all six activities; 6 qualifying resource items against a chance expectation of about 0.003 is far beyond what an unchanged process typically produces, and each shift is larger than about 999.5 of 1,000 random re-splits. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Limitations: the profiles show shares, not the mechanism — the evidence cannot distinguish a change in allocation rules from a change in which resources were available or in the mix of cases handled; A13 and A14 have identical profiles, so the six items are not six independent differences; and the anonymous codes allow no statement about roles or teams. No control-flow difference qualified at the configured thresholds, so the hypothesis is confined to resource allocation and implies no structural change. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
